title: The Tunguska Event: The Forest Fell, So Where Is the Crater?
description:
Just after 7 a.m. on June 30, 1908, a huge bang rang out over Siberia. A man 64 kilometers away was thrown from his chair, about 2,000 square kilometers of forest fell outward, and that night the sky glowed from Siberia to Europe.

This episode works through the file in the order the facts came to light: what the local papers and an observatory left on record at the time, the 1921 trip that never got there, the standing dead trees found at the very center in 1927, the old stump that surfaced when a round pit in the bog was drained, the decades when comets, alien ships and black holes took turns, and what a 2025 journal review traced: the most-quoted "80 million trees" was never counted. Last comes today's explanation, and four things that are still unsettled.

Versions that circulate are always labeled as such; where there is no conclusion, we say so. Sources for every number, year and quote are listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures appear as cartoon characters, unnamed and not drawn to resemble anyone; living or recent people are not depicted.

Information as of 2026-10-10

chapters.pointing-at-the-ground: He drains a round pit in the bog

tg1a.text: June 30, 1908, a little after seven in the morning.

tg1b.text: On the porch of a Siberian trading post sat a man.

tg1c.text: Then a huge boom came from the far sky.

tg1d.text: It threw him off his chair.

tg1e.text: That sound later got a name: the Tunguska event.

tg1j.text: Starting that night, from Siberia to Europe, the sky glowed for several nights.

tg1p.text: In 1927, someone followed the fallen trees to the very center, looking for a crater.

tg1q.text: He drained a round pit in the bog. What would be underneath?

tg1r.text: In 1946, a work of fiction told of that very blast.

tg1s.text: In 2025, someone chased down the most-quoted number.

tg1n.text: So where did whatever fell that morning land?

tg2a.text: After those bright nights, a local Siberian paper ran the story.

tg2b.text: The paper came out on July 12, twelve days after that morning.

tg2c.text: On Russia's old calendar, that morning was dated June 17.

tg2e.text: The same day it asked correspondents for sightings.

tg2f.text: So 'nobody knew for 19 years' is wrong.

tg2j.text: Witnesses said tents nearer the blast shook.

tg2k.text: Nearby Evenki wouldn't talk to outsiders at first.

tg2l.text: They believed the god Ogdy had come down.

tg2m.text: News was out. Why did nobody go in?

tg2o.text: In 1921, the Soviet Academy of Sciences sent a geologist.

tg2p.text: His name was Kulik, born August 19, 1883.

tg2r.text: Reach it, and he'd dig out the iron.

tg2s.text: One reason no one went into that forest: it was impassable.

tg2t.text: That year and the next, he got no farther than Kansk.

tg2w.text: Back home, he kept at it.

tg2x.text: Six years later, he set out again.

tg3a.text: On the 1927 trip from the opening, he finally made it.

tg3b.text: First, he saw the fallen trees.

tg3d.text: Trunks lay like spokes of a wheel, all pointing out.

tg3e.text: Follow their line inward to reach the center.

tg3g.text: The area later measured about 2,150 square kilometers.

tg3h.text: And not a circle, but a butterfly shape.

tg3i.text: But that's not the strangest part.

tg3j.text: At the center, the trees still stood.

tg3k.text: Branches and leaves stripped, bark gone.

tg3l.text: Standing there one by one, like a row of telegraph poles.

tg3m.text: He called the dead trees the telegraph-pole forest.

tg3n.text: They also showed signs of burning.

tg3p.text: At the center was a bog.

tg3q.text: Not just at the center: to this day, none within 15,000 square kilometers.

tg3v.text: Search Tunguska today, and the top number is 80 million fallen trees.

tg3w.text: We'll return to where it came from.

tg3x.text: So where did the thing that flattened this forest go?

tg4a.text: Kulik's answer: it was still underground.

tg4b.text: He thought the bog hid the big crater.

tg4c.text: The bog had some round hollows.

tg4d.text: He saw them as small impact pits.

tg4e.text: One was called the Suslov crater.

tg4f.text: He chose to drain the opening's round pit.

tg4g.text: Men and tools, all into the bog.

tg4h.text: Bit by bit, the water went down.

tg4i.text: At the bottom of the pit, what showed was not iron.

tg4m.text: the spot was right; his idea was not.

tg4o.text: For three years he mostly hunted iron fragments.

tg4p.text: He found none, and to this day no one has found a large piece.

tg4r.text: But they can't be tied to the blast for sure.

tg4s.text: Not far from that bog, there's also a lake: Lake Cheko.

tg4t.text: It became a clue only much later. More on it soon.

tg2h.text: Seismic and barometer records waited long, too.

tg2i.text: Only in 1925 and 1930 were they linked back to that morning.

tg4u.text: While he was still digging, others began searching the sky.

tg4v.text: In 1930, someone proposed it was a comet.

tg4w.text: The comet theory leaned on the bright nights.

tg4ad.text: By this theory, the glow came from the comet tail's scattered dust.

tg4y.text: Who said it first? Two sources disagree.

tg4z.text: Kulik didn't live to see an answer.

tg4aa.text: After war broke out in 1941, he joined the militia.

tg4ab.text: Wounded and captured, he died on April 14, 1942.

tg4ac.text: From setting out to his death, he gave this 21 years.

tg5a.text: Four years after he died, the story changed.

tg5b.text: In 1946, a Soviet magazine ran a work of fiction.

tg5c.text: In the fiction from the opening, an alien nuclear spaceship caused the blast.

tg5g.text: that the first to explain no crater with a midair blast was this fiction.

tg5h.text: In the late 1950s, it even got its own civilian expedition.

tg5k.text: In 1973, someone proposed a small black hole.

tg5m.text: A paper refuted the black hole one a year later.

tg5p.text: Tesla's death ray? Nobody suggested it until after the Cold War.

tg5r.text: But the most-quoted number is a bigger problem.

tg6b.text: In 2025, a journal review traced where it came from.

tg6e.text: That takes the fallen area first.

tg6g.text: Then turned area into a tree count.

tg6h.text: What the search from the opening found: that area was wrong.

tg6i.text: The measured area was only about a quarter of what he assumed.

tg6k.text: So 80 million trees was too high from the start.

tg6m.text: The number was copied, paper after paper.

tg6t.text: Eventually it was treated as fact needing no citation.

tg6u.text: Over 90 years on, videos and articles still use it.

tg6w.text: The record backs only the area.

tg6x.text: So what made that butterfly shape we just saw?

tg7a.text: That shape was made by an object tens of meters across.

tg7b.text: The answer to the opening question: it entered the air and burst midair.

tg7e.text: A 2019 simulation put it at 10 to 14 kilometers.

tg7f.text: The shock wave pushed down and outward.

tg7g.text: That's how those outward-fallen trees went down.

tg7i.text: So the crater Kulik sought at the center never formed at all.

tg7k.text: In TNT terms, estimates run from 3 million to 30 million tons.

tg7l.text: Some simulations push it to the low end. Still no conclusion.

tg7n.text: In 2007, one team said its bed looked like a crater.

tg7o.text: In 2008, another team said: highly unlikely.

tg7p.text: A 2017 study: sediment older than the blast.

tg7q.text: No conclusion on the lakebed. Did the blast kill anyone?

tg7s.text: A 2019 paper: at least 30 people in and near the zone.

tg7t.text: Of them, at least three died from it.

tg7u.text: One source lists only two unverified reports.

tg7r.text: Did anyone die? No conclusion either.

tg7v.text: Whether it was a stony asteroid or a comet fragment is still debated.

tg7aa.text: Many people saw it and filmed it.

tg7ac.text: From that morning to now: 118 years.

tg7ae.text: Where did you first hear of Tunguska?

tg7af.text: This channel sticks to the record. Subscribe to open files with us.
